picks.title: 'MemoMind One' Kickstarter Hits $1M, Making a Strong Case for Camera-less Display Glasses
picks.excerpt: XGIMI's MemoMind One crossed $1M on Kickstarter with 20 days still to run, on a deliberately camera-less display-glasses design. The result reads as a market signal that buyers want the heads-up display and AI assist without the social cost of a face-mounted camera.
picks.rationale: Hard money proving the camera is the liability, not the feature — the clearest market verdict yet on how to spec AI eyewear.

picks.title: Could Meta Ray-Bans be banned in Europe? EU regulators dial up the pressure on smart glasses
picks.excerpt: EU regulators are turning up pressure on camera-equipped smart glasses while China issues a manufacturer code of conduct and South Korea bars them from exam halls. Recording-indicator and consent design is becoming a hardware requirement, not a nicety.
picks.rationale: Turns consent and recording-indicator design from a nicety into a shipping requirement across three major markets at once.

picks.title: Apple Rumored to Launch Three New 'Ultra' Products by Early Next Year
picks.excerpt: Gurman reports three 'Ultra' products landing between late 2026 and early 2027, including AirPods Ultra with tiny infrared camera 'eyes' that feed Siri's Visual Intelligence. Camera-in-earbud would put a seeing sensor on the head without the glasses form factor.
picks.rationale: Moves the seeing sensor from the face to the ear — a form-factor dodge around the exact camera backlash the other picks describe.

picks.title: This Startup Will Pay You $50 to Let AI Read Your Mind
picks.excerpt: San Francisco startup Conduit is paying people $50-$55 to wear an electrode-studded headband and talk to an AI for two hours, collecting training data for a noninvasive thought-to-machine input channel. It is an early look at the input layer after voice and gesture.
picks.rationale: A first look at the input modality after voice and gesture, and at how the training data for it is actually being bought.

picks.title: I turned my phone into an AI agent powered by my local LLM, and it installed software on its own
picks.excerpt: A hands-on turning an Android phone into an autonomous agent running entirely on a local LLM — to the point it installed software on its own. Shows what on-device inference plus tool-calling actually feels like as an interface, and where it breaks.
picks.rationale: Reproducible hands-on showing what an on-device agent interface actually feels like — including the moments it oversteps.
